# 8 Check Self Score

## Question: Fix

Our question aims to help the Governor’s office identify which Virginia localities carry the highest severe accident frequency over time and where to direct resources to reduce it. This check is rated Fix. The dataset’s Severity variable (1–4) is a proxy that measures the impact on traffic flow (short vs. long delay) rather than direct accident severity. The question should be narrowed to prioritize areas for follow-up VDOT investigation to reduce accident delay. 

## Data: Pass

The data check passes because our question/dataset is based on Virginia car accidents and our dataset contains Virginia traffic records. We also investigate the accident severity, weather conditions, and location variables to compare accident patterns. The data covers different localities and years which allows our dashboard to filter through them and see changes over time.  

## Transformation: Fix

This check is rated as Fix. We have yet to do an independence check for the binomial confidence intervals in our dashboard. The Fix would check for near duplicative records (those with the same location and similar time frame of accident) and remove them. Furthermore, while M2 involves extensive data extraction checks to ensure we are always extracting the correct data, M3 added to the app reductions of the weather covariate into 5 core categories. We have yet to check these 5 to make sure there are no sudden drops of observations because of misspellings or near close weather names. 

## Inferential: Fix

This check is rated as Fix primarily because of the confidence interval section. The confidence intervals we calculated have an independence assumption. For example, if accidents are not independent (similar accidents located minutes apart in the same spot) then the binomial confidence interval is invalid. Additionally, for our confidence intervals involving the grouping of monthly rates/ratios into months, if there is auto-correlation in our months the independence assumption is violated.  A simple Fix is to run an autocorrelation test in R on our primary metrics. If we find autocorrelation, then confidence intervals may need to be adjusted accordingly. Additionally, we should Fix the binomial one by checking for near duplicative records and removing those that are in the same location and close in time frame. 

## Perceptual: Pass

The perceptual check passes because the dashboard communicates the data effectively through bar graphs and graph comparisons. All graphs are not truncated, use color blind friendly colors, and the information follows the appropriate visualization channel. Our map also uses a normalized measure of severe rates to compare the different localities.  

## Communication: Fix

The communication check needs a fix by defining severity and correctly labeling the observations. Although our chart titles, subtitles, captions, and screen-reader summaries are clear, we need to provide more context for the readers. We will do this by including a brief summary of our data, making sure the chart labels are accurate, and the app's (titles, KPIs, and axes) should be relabeled to identify localities and corridors with the highest high-traffic-delay crash rates (per 100k residents and high delay crash share). 

## Operational: Fix

The operational check needs a fix because we do not identify the freshness of the data or the data coverage period. Our freshness needs to be clarified to reflect the most recent information and updates. We will add a disclosure that our data was collected from 2016 to 2023 and an artifact version history (R version and last update of dashboard).  

## Downstream decision: Fix

This check is rated as a Fix primarily because of how we edited our question in M3 to include a decision of where Virginia's resources are best utilized to reduce accidents. In this case, we do not pre-define the threshold that triggers a triage decision, or what boundary would cause a resource decision (is it 40% severity rate, or some 100k ratio that is the threshold?) The fix would be to predefine what a decision would trigger a triage resource allocation rule (is it 50% severe rate) and restructure our graph 3 to correspond to that rate.

## What is our is weakest check?

Our weakest check is communication because we define and use a variable call severity in the dashboard, but miscommunicate what this means in our dashboard. A governor reading this might think worst financial burden and jump to the wrong conclusion where instead we are showcasing only traffic delay.

# The Evidence of Analytic Work Story

The AI functioned as a primary dashboard constructor and to build the code for changes we specified. From AI results, we changed the first summary page to be more statistically accurate and simpler by: making sure that the confidence intervals have enough sample size and that their graph view optional, label changes to make each graph relate to the question and changed the default filter to be all localities and not top 5 in population. Finally, we removed unnecessary prediction intervals and made default family-wise error corrections on the confidence intervals to simplify the user's view and make the view more statistically accurate.  

# Disclosure statement drafted in the form it will take in the final package.

Matthew led data extraction, executed a join to census data, and initial data validation checks to look for no unmatched census values and timestamp and severity integrity checks. Maria led the exploratory data analysis and dashboard validation to make sure the confidence intervals are accurate. Both members conducted peer interviews and reviewed all updates/final products. The AI tools used were Genimi and ChatGPT in the fall of 2026, for creating the dashboard, data dictionary, and for formatting different changes such as making the charts into a button and updating the interactive behavior across all three pages. We independently verify our work and have the AI log and Individual Contribution Ledger in our appendix.
